passage:
At Kishore's new school, Vikas mimicked his accent when he read aloud, and a few others snickered. Kishore's cheeks burned. For a month he swapped his kurta for a trendy tee, clipped his vowels and said "bro" every second sentence. It won him a seat at the popular lunch bench, but by evening he felt like he was wearing a costume.

One weekend he went home and heard his grandmother singing in their mother tongue. He felt proud of the words, the recipes and the festival his family kept. He also noticed that pride did not mean thinking anyone else was lesser.

On Monday he told the class teacher about the mimicking, and the teacher spoke to Vikas that same day. He also found two friends in the chess club who liked the way he explained his openings in his own voice.

Tanuja sat behind him. She got up at five every day to help at her family's tea stall before school. Kishore wanted to know what that was like. Instead of guessing, he asked, "What is your morning like?" and listened while she explained the leaves, the regular customers and the way she did homework on the bus. He walked home realising his world was one of many.

qa.q: At what time did Tanuja get up every day?
qa.a: She got up at five every day.

qa.q: How did Kishore's early attempt to fit in differ from what he found later with his chess friends and with Tanuja?
qa.a: At first he changed his clothes and speech to sit at the popular bench, but felt like he was wearing a costume. Later, proud of his roots, he found friends who liked his own voice and asked Tanuja about her mornings, learning instead of guessing.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when Vikas mimicked his accent?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and stung. His cheeks burned.

qa.q: What helped Kishore when the mimicking happened?
qa.a: He told the class teacher, who spoke to Vikas that same day, and he found friends in the chess club.

grounding: A teenager changes how he talks and dresses to fit in after being mimicked, then draws on pride in his own roots and curiosity about a classmate's very different life.

passage:
Sumit Sir tore Vishal's history essay in half while the whole room watched. "This is what happens when someone thinks he is clever." Nobody breathed. Shame and rage swirled in Vishal's chest, but he kept his face still, picked up his bag and got through the period. At home he told Papa. Together they wrote down the date and the exact words. Two days later Vishal went with Papa to Principal Saurabh and read from his notes, calmly, facts only. He had not posted a word online. The principal listened, thanked him and met Sumit Sir that same week. It had never been about Vishal's worth.

Meanwhile his English teacher believed in him. "You can write." Vishal worked at night to earn that respect. He noticed his effort dipped whenever they were absent, so he began keeping a private notebook of stories, for himself.

By Class 12 he could see that the strict physics teacher had pushed him well, and he went to say thank you. Still, he knew that a method working on him once did not make harshness good.

qa.q: Whom did Vishal go to see with Papa?
qa.a: He went with Papa to Principal Saurabh.

qa.q: How did Vishal handle the teacher who humiliated him, compared with the teacher who believed in him and the strict teacher he later thanked?
qa.a: After the insult he kept his composure, told Papa and reported the facts calmly through the principal. The English teacher's belief pushed him to work, and he built his own drive with a notebook. Later he thanked the strict physics teacher, while knowing that a method working on him once did not make harshness good.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when Sumit Sir tore his history essay in half?
qa.a: He felt shame and rage, though he kept his face still.

qa.q: Why did Vishal and Papa write down the date and the exact words before seeing the principal?
qa.a: So Vishal could report calmly with facts, instead of only with anger.

grounding: One student meets a humiliating teacher, a teacher whose belief he works to earn, a principal he trusts with a factual report, and later gratitude toward a strict teacher.

passage:
Papa knelt to help Dolma with the top button of her coat, doing only the tricky loop and letting her push the rest through. "Thank you, Papa!" she said, pleased at how much she could do herself.

At the school gate her big sister Trisha swung Dolma's heavy bag onto her back. "You owe me a sweet," Trisha said. Dolma frowned, unsure. Did she have a sweet? She said "thank you." Later, when Trisha's shoelace came loose, Dolma crouched and tied it as best she could, in her own time. At home Mummy told Trisha, "Helping is a gift. No sweets needed." Trisha shrugged and tucked the bag on its hook.

In class, as her sums got harder, Dolma kept calling, "Miss Elizabeth, can you do it for me?" She was afraid of getting them wrong. Miss Elizabeth crouched down. "Try one step, and I will be right here." Dolma wrote one number, then a second, glancing up each time. By the end she had finished the row and beamed.

qa.q: What did Papa help Dolma with?
qa.a: He helped her with the top button of her coat.

qa.q: How did the help from Papa and Miss Elizabeth differ from the help from Trisha at the gate?
qa.a: Papa and Miss Elizabeth helped just enough so Dolma could finish herself. Trisha attached a price with "You owe me a sweet", leaving Dolma unsure, until Dolma helped back in her own time.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when Trisha said she owed a sweet?
qa.a: She felt unsure and frowned, wondering whether she had a sweet to give.

qa.q: What did Miss Elizabeth do that helped Dolma with her sums?
qa.a: She said, "Try one step, and I will be right here," so Dolma could write the numbers herself while knowing help was near.

grounding: A young child is helped by a parent who does just enough, a sibling who asks for payment, and a teacher who turns fearful asking into one small step.

passage:
Yamini's jokes about Vaibhav's ears got laughs in the yard. She had found a way to feel big: if the joke was about him, nobody made one about her. At home, her cousins called her "chubby cheeks", and she hated it. Nazia laughed along the first time. Afterwards her stomach lurched and she felt sick with guilt. That evening she kept picturing Vaibhav's face.

Next morning Vaibhav flinched when Yamini walked past, his shoulders drawn up near his ears. It was the flinch that made her pause. She had thought it was funny, but now her chest went tight. It was not pride she felt, but discomfort. She teased no one that day.

At lunch Nazia found Vaibhav by the tap. "I laughed yesterday, and I should not have. I am sorry." Vaibhav shrugged. "Okay." When Yamini started again by the door, Nazia said, "Not funny. I am not joining." Yamini rolled her eyes and left.

The following day Yamini walked over to Vaibhav. "I made fun of your ears because I was scared of being teased myself. It was not a joke. I am sorry." She sat with a kinder group at lunch, and found she did not have to be cruel to belong.

qa.q: What did Yamini's jokes target?
qa.a: Her jokes targeted Vaibhav's ears.

qa.q: How did Yamini's reason for teasing compare with Nazia's reason for laughing, and what did each do after seeing the effect?
qa.a: Yamini teased because she dreaded being teased herself and wanted to feel big. Nazia simply laughed along, then felt sick with guilt. After Vaibhav flinched, Yamini stopped and later apologised, and Nazia apologised and refused to join again.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling that evening after laughing along at Vaibhav?
qa.a: She felt guilty and sick, and kept picturing Vaibhav's face.

qa.q: What could Yamini do about her fear of being teased, instead of teasing first?
qa.a: She could build real confidence and sit with kinder friends, as she did.

grounding: Children around one teased boy show a girl who attacks first from insecurity, a friend who laughs along and regrets it, and the boy's visible fear that ends the teasing.

passage:
Mohit's manager gave the team-lead role to someone with less experience, and heat rushed up Mohit's neck. He waited for the worst of the heat to fade by walking to the stairwell and back. That night he wrote down the projects he had led, then asked for a private talk. "Can you explain the decision?" The manager gave a vague answer, and Mohit decided to watch the next quarter before choosing whether to stay.

Lalit, in sales, was told by the same manager to promise customers a delivery date that could not be met. Lalit liked the manager and felt loyal, but he said, "I cannot tell them that. I will give them the real date and offer a discount." The manager glared. Lalit held firm.

At Monday meetings the manager belittled Ganga's presentations. "Did you even try?" Ganga's face flushed and she felt unsafe. It was not her fault. After every meeting she jotted down the date and the words, and eventually took them to HR and a senior mentor.

Ganga also knew one promotion decision had been unfair to a colleague, but she hesitated to speak because she needed the job. She found two colleagues who agreed, and wrote a calm email listing facts. She knew silence has its price too.

qa.q: Where did Mohit walk to let his anger pass?
qa.a: He walked to the stairwell and back.

qa.q: How did Lalit's stance on loyalty differ from Ganga's response to fear about speaking up?
qa.a: Lalit put honesty to customers above loyalty to the manager and refused a false date. Ganga, afraid for her job, weighed the risk, found two allies and wrote a calm email, knowing silence has its price too.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when the manager belittled her presentations?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and unsafe, though she knew it was not her fault.

qa.q: What did Mohit do with his anger about the promotion?
qa.a: He waited for the worst of the heat to fade by walking, wrote down the projects he had led, and asked for a private explanation.

grounding: A manager's unfair choices bring anger over a passed-over role, a conflict between loyalty and honesty, fear of speaking up, and humiliation in meetings.

passage:
For the first month Varun showered Mehak with attention: long messages at 2 a.m., surprise flowers, "you are everything." When she said she needed one evening a week for herself, he went silent for three days. Mehak noticed the swing, and began to judge him by what he did steadily, not by the grand gestures.

Then he began denying things. "I never said that," he told her, about a plan he had promised. "You are so sensitive." Mehak started writing things down in her notes app. When she showed the entries to a friend, the friend said, "That is what you told me that day. You are not imagining it." She recognised the doubt for what it was.

Slowly Varun made her feel guilty for seeing friends, and her Sunday calls to her cousins tailed off. Madhuri texted, "I miss you. Chai tomorrow?" Mehak kept that one tie alive and went. Over tea she said aloud what was happening, and Madhuri stayed beside her, then went with her that week to the college counsellor.

Varun, for his part, admitted to a friend that he kept tabs because he was frightened of being left. The friend told him that was not love. He booked an appointment with a counsellor too.

qa.q: What did Madhuri text Mehak?
qa.a: Madhuri texted, "I miss you. Chai tomorrow?"

qa.q: How did Varun's early attention differ from his behaviour after Mehak asked for time to herself, and what did Mehak do about the doubt and the distance from friends?
qa.a: Early on came intense adoration, and once she asked for an evening alone came silence, denial and guilt about friends. Mehak judged him by his steady behaviour, wrote things down, checked with a friend and kept one tie alive with Madhuri.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when Varun called her so sensitive after denying what he had promised?
qa.a: She felt doubtful and unsure of her own memory, until her notes and a friend confirmed what happened.

qa.q: What could Varun do about his fear of being left?
qa.a: He could admit it, as he did to a friend, and work on it with a counsellor instead of tracking Mehak and calling it love.

grounding: A partner's intense adoration turns cold when limits are set, followed by denial of events and pulling away from friends, alongside the partner's own fear of abandonment.
